++++
+title = "CAM fundamentals"
+description = "The core machining challenges behind a good program, and what CamCraft does about each."

++++
+
+A toolpath is only as good as the machining decisions behind it. These pages
+explain the challenges every CAM job meets, in general machining terms, and
+then say plainly what CamCraft does about each one: which setting carries it,
+what the program gate checks, and what is left to you at the machine.
+
+The principles are general machining knowledge: the standard formulas and
+the habits a shop passes on. They are not feeds-and-speeds tables. CamCraft
+does not know your machine, your material lot or your fixture, so where a
+page says "check", the check is yours. Where CamCraft has no feature for
+something, the page says so.
+
+1. [Feeds and speeds](@/guide/fundamentals/feeds-and-speeds.md)
+2. [Tool selection and reach](@/guide/fundamentals/tool-selection.md)
+3. [Toolpath strategy](@/guide/fundamentals/toolpath-strategy.md)

+

@@ -0,0 +1,44 @@
++++
+title = "Chip evacuation and coolant"
+description = "Getting chips out of deep cuts, and the coolant settings CamCraft writes."
+weight = 5
++++
+
+## The principles
+
+**Chips must leave the cut.** A chip that stays in a deep pocket or slot gets
+cut again. That heats the edge, scars the surface and can jam the tool. The
+risk grows with depth, with narrow slots (where chips have nowhere to go) and
+with sticky materials.
+
+**Deep pockets and slots.** Cut in steps of limited depth rather than the
+full flute length. A slot gives chips only the flute channel to escape, so use a
+lighter cut, a lower stepdown or a tool with fewer flutes.
+
+**Peck drilling.** In a deep hole, the drill retracts part way, or fully, between
+pecks so chips are cleared and coolant can reach the tip. A hole deeper than
+a few diameters usually needs it.
+
+**Air, mist or flood.** Flood coolant cools and flushes chips, and suits steel
+and deep cuts. Mist is lighter. A blast of air clears chips and avoids the
+thermal shock of intermittent coolant on carbide, a common choice for
+aluminium and plastics. Through-tool coolant delivers fluid at the tip
+of a deep hole.
+
+## What CamCraft does
+
+- **Peck and deep drilling.** The drill kind offers spot, drill, peck, deep,
+  tap and bore cycles, with a peck depth, and a dwell at the bottom.
+- **Stepdown** limits depth per level in pockets and slots.
+- **Coolant** is a per-operation choice: **Off**, **Flood** (the default),
+  **Mist** or **Through tool**. The post switches the machine's own code
+  on for the operation. A choice the machine states no code for, such as
+  through-tool coolant on a machine without it, blocks the post by name,
+  rather than being written as a guess. Coolant modes are declared by the machine
+  file; see [Machine types](https://neotech.github.io/Camcraft/guide/machines/).
+
+CamCraft has no separate "air blast" mode: the four choices above are
+the whole list. If you run air blast, set the operation to **Off** and
+turn it on at the machine, or add the code by hand after posting. CamCraft
+does not model chips, so it cannot tell you that a slot will pack. Read the
+first cut.

@@ -0,0 +1,93 @@
++++
+title = "Feeds and speeds"
+description = "Surface speed, chip load, engagement and chip thinning, and where CamCraft stores and limits them."
+weight = 1
++++
+
+Feeds and speeds are the two numbers that decide whether a cut is fast,
+clean and survivable: how fast the tool spins, and how fast it moves.
+
+## The principles
+
+**Surface speed** is how fast the cutting edge travels through the material
+at the tool's outer diameter. It depends on the work material and the tool
+material, not on the tool size. **Chip load** (feed per tooth, `fz`) is how
+much material each flute takes per revolution. Too little rubs instead of
+cutting and wears the edge; too much overloads it.
+
+The two formulas that turn them into machine settings:
+
+- spindle speed: `n = Vc x 1000 / (pi x D)`, with `Vc` in m/min, `D` in mm and
+  `n` in rpm (in inch units, `n = Vc x 12 / (pi x D)` with `Vc` in feet per
+  minute and `D` in inches);
+- feed rate: `vf = fz x z x n`, with `z` the number of flutes.
+
+**Engagement.** Radial engagement (`ae`, the stepover) is how much of the
+diameter is in the cut sideways; axial engagement (`ap`, the stepdown) is how
+deep. Heavy axial depth with light radial engagement is the usual way to use
+the full flute length.
+
+**Chip thinning.** When the radial engagement is less than half the
+diameter, each flute leaves the cut before it has taken a full-thickness
+chip. The real chip is thinner than `fz`. For a square-shouldered cut the
+ratio is `2 x sqrt(r - r^2)`, with `r = ae / D`. To keep the intended chip
+thickness at light stepovers, raise the programmed feed by the inverse of that
+ratio. The compensation has a limit: at very light stepovers the factor runs
+away, so it is held.
+
+**Plunge and ramp feeds.** Plunging loads the tool axially, where an end mill
+is weakest and chips cannot escape, so plunge feed is much lower than cutting
+feed. A ramp or helix entry spreads the descent over a longer path.
+
+**Reading the cut.** A steady, even sound is right. A scream or chatter means
+speed or engagement is wrong. Chips should come off as clean, uniformly
+coloured curls. Blue or dark chips in steel, or melted, welded chips in
+aluminium, mean too much heat for the feed. These are cues for the first
+cuts, not numbers.
+
+**A less rigid machine** needs less engagement and a lower feed before it
+needs a lower speed. Lighter radial engagement is usually the first change.
+
+## What CamCraft does
+
+On an operation's **Feeds** tab:
+
+- **Spindle speed** is shown and editable as rpm, or as surface speed
+  through the tool's diameter: m/min in a millimetre document, surface
+  feet per minute (SFM) in an inch one. The speed lives on the tool.
+- **Feed** and **Plunge feed** are separate numbers on the operation.
+- **Climb milling** is a check box (see
+  [Toolpath strategy](@/guide/fundamentals/toolpath-strategy.md)).
+- The **Cutting data** group holds the document's workpiece material, the
+  tool's edge material (HSS or carbide) and flute count. With all three
+  stated, **Suggest feeds & speeds** shows a starting rpm and feed from
+  the formulas above. Nothing changes until you click **Apply
+  suggestion**, and the apply is one undoable step.
+- The suggestion's numbers come from a small built-in table of workpiece
+  groups (steel, stainless, cast iron, non-ferrous, plastics) with
+  conservative starting values. They are a starting point, not a limit.
+  The table does not speak for every tool kind: it says so by name when it
+  cannot suggest.
+- Chip thinning compensation is applied only where the operation states an
+  optimal engagement load. Adaptive clearing does.
+- Lathe tools can state a constant surface speed and a feed per revolution;
+  the post then writes constant surface speed with a maximum-rpm clamp.
+
+**Limits CamCraft enforces.** The suggestion is clamped to the mounted
+machine's stated spindle range and feed ceiling, and each clamp is named
+in the suggestion. Independently, the program gate refuses to post an
+operation whose tool runs above or below the machine's stated rpm, and one
+whose estimated spindle power exceeds the machine's stated power (only when
+the machine, material, flutes and engagement are all stated; CamCraft makes no
+claim from an unstated number).
+
+A lathe setup can also state a **workholding rpm limit** (the chuck or
+collet rating). Under constant surface speed the rpm ceiling becomes the
+lowest of the machine's, the tool's and the workholding's. Under constant
+rpm, an operation over that limit is refused by name, not capped, because
+the cut was planned at that speed. The limit is lathe-only; mill setups
+have no equivalent setting. See [Setups](@/guide/setups.md) and
+[Workholding](https://neotech.github.io/Camcraft/guide/workholding/).
+
+CamCraft does not measure sound or chip colour and does not model machine
+rigidity. The first cut is where you learn whether the numbers fit.

@@ -0,0 +1,65 @@
++++
+title = "Post and machine quirks"
+description = "The start block, units, tool-centre-point output and checking the first program on a new machine."
+weight = 8
++++
+
+## The principles
+
+**A post is a dialect.** The same toolpath is written differently for
+different controls: how a tool change is called, how a canned cycle is
+written, which words a control accepts on one line.
+
+**A safe start block.** A program should not depend on what the last one
+left behind. The first block states the modes explicitly: absolute
+positioning (G90), cutter compensation off (G40), tool length compensation
+cancelled (G49), canned cycles cancelled (G80), the work offset (G54 and its
+relatives) and the plane. Then the tool change and length offset.
+
+**Inch or millimetre.** A control left in inch by the last program reads
+millimetre numbers as inches, a 25-times error. The unit is stated by G20 (inch)
+or G21 (millimetre), in a block of its own before any motion, per RS-274.
+
+**Tool centre point (TCP) or not.** On a machine with tilting axes, the
+control can either hold the tool tip at the programmed point while the axes
+tilt (TCP, also called RTCP or TCPM, with a word such as G43.4), or the
+program can be written in terms of the axis positions. A three-axis machine has
+neither.
+
+**A new machine's first program.** Cut air first. Check the units, the
+work offset and tool length numbers against what the machine holds, the
+spindle direction, and how it handles a tool change. Then proceed to
+[proving out](@/guide/fundamentals/proving-out.md).
+
+## What CamCraft does
+
+- **Built-in posts** are scripts: Fanuc, Haas, Siemens 840D, Heidenhain,
+  Mazak, Tormach PathPilot, Makera Carvera and Fanuc Lathe, and you can load your own.
+  The setup chooses its post and machine; see [Setups](@/guide/setups.md).
+- **Start blocks.** At each operation the Fanuc-family post writes absolute
+  mode, the work offset, cutter compensation off, length offset
+  cancelled and canned cycles cancelled, then the tool change and length
+  offset. The Haas post also states the XY plane.
+- **Units.** The Fanuc and Haas posts write G21 (millimetres) in a block of
+  its own before any motion. The Carvera firmware is millimetres only, and
+  the post raises a warning when the machine file is in inches. Making the program unit a
+  document setting is an open issue (#902), so for an inch control check the
+  first block of the file. See
+  [Units and coordinates](https://neotech.github.io/Camcraft/guide/units-and-coordinates/).
+- **Tilted output.** The Fanuc post arms its tool-centre-point mode (G43.4)
+  when the path tilts the tool. The intermediate stream is specified so that a
+  post that keeps the machine prismatic refuses a tilted record rather
+  than reinterpret it ([the stream
+  spec](https://github.com/NeoTech/Camcraft/blob/main/docs/CNC-INTERMEDIATE.md)).
+  See [Machine types](https://neotech.github.io/Camcraft/guide/machines/) and
+  [Multi-axis operations](https://neotech.github.io/Camcraft/guide/operations-multiaxis/).
+- **Machine files** state facts (axis travel, spindle range, tool changer,
+  rigid tapping, coolant codes), and the program is checked against the
+  facts stated. A machine file is not a guarantee that a real machine is
+  safe: check its numbers against the manual. Documenting a new machine is
+  covered in the [machine onboarding
+  guide](https://github.com/NeoTech/Camcraft/blob/main/docs/MACHINE-ONBOARDING.md).
+
+Post output is always a first draft. Read the first program line by line
+against your control's manual before running it. See
+[Posting](@/guide/posting.md).

@@ -0,0 +1,53 @@
++++
+title = "Proving out a program"
+description = "Simulation, verify and what its refusals mean, a dry run, single block and the first-article check."
+weight = 7
++++
+
+## The principles
+
+A program is a claim that a path is safe and removes the right material. Prove it in
+stages, each one cheaper than a crash:
+
+1. **Simulate** the stock being cut, and compare the result with the model.
+2. **Dry run** at the machine with the spindle off and the tool well above
+   the part (for example with Z offset raised), watching the whole path for
+   anything unexpected.
+3. **Single block** the first cuts: one line at a time, with feed and
+   rapid overrides turned down, a hand on the stop, watching distance to go.
+4. **First article.** Cut one part, measure it, and only then run the batch.
+
+Software checks the model, stock, tool and machine facts it was given. It
+cannot see a clamp you forgot to enter or a wrong tool length.
+
+## What CamCraft does
+
+- **Simulate** plays the program against the stock. **Deviate** colours
+  where material is left or where the program cut into the part, and **Frame
+  rest** and **Frame gouge** go to the worst spot of each. **Paths** shows
+  the cached toolpaths together.
+- **Verify** runs at **Post**. It writes the program only when every
+  operation is generated and current, none carries a warning, and the whole
+  program passes: no gouge into the part, no move strikes a fixture, no rapid
+  runs through stock, and no move exceeds a limit the mounted machine states.
+  See [Posting](@/guide/posting.md).
+- **What a refusal means.** The message names the operation and the
+  problem. A gouge refusal means the simulated cutter removed model
+  material; a warning refusal names the flagged moves, which are marked in
+  the viewport. The table of common messages is in
+  [Reading a refusal](@/guide/refusals.md) and
+  [Troubleshooting](https://neotech.github.io/Camcraft/guide/troubleshooting/).
+- **Why refuse rather than warn.** A warning on a dialog gets clicked
+  through and the program is posted anyway. Where the output could drive
+  the tool into the part or a fixture, CamCraft writes nothing, and leaves any
+  existing file untouched. The two named exceptions are advisory and show on the
+  operation without holding the post: a scallop note (a finish quality
+  matter) and a probe search distance.
+- **"Not judged" is not "fine".** If a check cannot run to completion, for
+  example a hidden-material scan that hits its budget, that is reported as
+  not judged and holds the post, never counted as zero.
+- **Setup sheets** list each setup's tools in change order, with estimated
+  time, for the operator.
+
+A green gate is not a guarantee. Run the dry run, single block and
+first-article steps above on any new program.

@@ -0,0 +1,53 @@
++++
+title = "Rigidity, chatter and deflection"
+description = "Why long tools, thin walls and loose setups cut badly, and what to change."
+weight = 4
++++
+
+## The principles
+
+**Tool length to diameter.** A tool bends like a cantilever: deflection
+grows with the cube of its stick-out and falls with the fourth power of its
+diameter. Beyond roughly four times its diameter in stick-out a tool needs
+lighter cuts, and beyond six or so it needs much lighter ones. A deflected
+tool cuts a tapered wall, leaving the part wider at the bottom than the top.
+
+**Thin walls and floors.** A thin wall flexes away from the tool, springs back
+and then gets cut again, which gives chatter, poor size and a rough finish. A
+thin floor does the same under axial load.
+
+**Leave stock for stiffness, and finish it last.** Rough while the part is
+still a thick, stiff block. Leave a finishing allowance, and cut the thin
+features to size in a final light pass, ideally in several shallow passes so
+the wall is supported by uncut material below the tool.
+
+**Part movement.** Cutting releases stress in the material, and clamping can
+distort a thin part. Roughing both sides before finishing either, and
+loosening and re-clamping lightly before a finish pass, are common ways to
+let it settle.
+
+**When it chatters.** Chatter is a self-excited vibration: a regular pitch
+and a wavy surface. Change one thing at a time: reduce radial engagement,
+shorten the stick-out, check the workholding, and then shift the spindle speed up or down a
+little (the speed that avoids a resonance is found by trying). Lower feed with the same speed
+usually makes it worse because the chip gets too thin.
+
+## What CamCraft does
+
+- **Stock to leave** on the Passes tab is the finishing allowance: roughing
+  stops short of the model by that amount, and a later operation finishes it.
+  Order the finish last; see
+  [Order of operations](https://neotech.github.io/Camcraft/guide/order-of-operations/).
+- **Contour tabs** (tab count, width and height) keep a profiled part
+  attached to the stock while its outline is cut.
+- **Stepover, stepdown and engagement** are per operation, so a light finish
+  pass on a thin wall is a separate operation with its own settings.
+- **Holders and stick-out** are stored on the tool, and collisions with them
+  are checked ([Tool selection](@/guide/fundamentals/tool-selection.md)).
+- **Workholding** and fixtures belong to the setup, and fixture collisions are
+  checked; see
+  [Workholding](https://neotech.github.io/Camcraft/guide/workholding/).
+
+CamCraft does not model tool deflection, part flex or chatter. It cannot warn
+you that a wall is too thin or a tool too long for a cut. That judgement,
+and the first-cut check, are yours.

@@ -0,0 +1,52 @@
++++
+title = "Surface finish and tolerance"
+description = "Stepover and scallop height, finish allowance, tolerance settings and holding size across setups."
+weight = 6
++++
+
+## The principles
+
+**Scallop height.** A ball or round-nosed tool stepping across a curved surface
+leaves a ridge between passes. For a ball of radius `R` and a stepover `s`,
+the ridge height is `h = R - sqrt(R^2 - (s/2)^2)`, about `s^2 / (8R)`. To hit
+a target height, the stepover is about `sqrt(8 R h)`. Halving the stepover
+cuts the ridge to a quarter, at twice the cutting time. On a flat floor
+with a flat end mill the stepover leaves no ridge, but it must still overlap.
+
+**Finish allowance.** Leave a small, even layer for the finish pass and
+cut it with a light, constant load. Too little and the finish tool rubs
+on uneven roughing; too much and it deflects.
+
+**Tolerance on the model against the toolpath.** The model has dimensional
+tolerances (what the drawing allows). The toolpath has a tolerance of its
+own: the largest error from approximating curves with short moves. Keep
+the toolpath tolerance well inside the part tolerance, say a fraction of
+it. A tighter value makes bigger programs and slower motion on the
+machine.
+
+**Holding tolerance across setups.** Each re-clamp adds position error.
+Features that must hold a tight relationship are best cut in the same
+setup, or located from a shared datum such as a bored hole or a machined
+face.
+
+## What CamCraft does
+
+- **Tolerance** is a setting on the milling operations. In the 3D finish
+  kinds it is the finish budget: lines and levels are spaced from it, so the
+  cusp stays within it. Where the stepover is **Auto**, CamCraft computes it
+  from the tolerance and the tool by the scallop law; a stated stepover
+  overrides it.
+- **A scallop check** on the 3D finish reports a ridge that stands outside
+  the tolerance. It is shown and named on the operation, but it is a
+  quality note and never blocks the post (it is neither a gouge nor a
+  collision).
+- **Stock to leave** is the finish allowance.
+- **Setups** carry stock and the work offset between setups (**Carry stock
+  and WCS over**), and a later setup can see the material an earlier one
+  left. See [Setups](@/guide/setups.md).
+
+CamCraft does not read tolerances from the model, and it does not check a
+programmed size against a drawing. The program is a path toward the
+model's geometry; whether the part meets the drawing is decided by
+measuring it. The setup accuracy across re-clamps is your workholding
+and touch-off, not something CamCraft can verify.

@@ -0,0 +1,55 @@
++++
+title = "Tool selection and reach"
+description = "Choosing the shortest tool that reaches, and how CamCraft checks reach and holders."
+weight = 2
++++
+
+## The principles
+
+**Shortest tool that reaches.** A tool's stiffness falls with the cube of
+its unsupported length. Use the shortest tool and the least stick-out (the
+length from the holder face to the tip) that reaches the deepest feature
+with clearance for the holder. See [Rigidity](@/guide/fundamentals/rigidity.md).
+
+**Diameter against the part.** A tool cannot cut an inside corner sharper
+than its own radius, so the smallest inside corner radius limits the largest
+tool for finishing that corner. Roughing can use a bigger tool; a smaller one
+then cleans up what is left (rest machining, see
+[Toolpath strategy](@/guide/fundamentals/toolpath-strategy.md)). In a
+narrow pocket the tool must also fit the narrowest width with room to move.
+
+**Flutes and material.** Fewer flutes leave more room for chips, which suits
+soft, gummy material and deep slots. More flutes allow a higher feed at the
+same chip load and give a finer finish in harder material. Carbide runs
+faster and stiffer than HSS but chips more easily under shock.
+
+**Holder clearance.** The holder is wider than the cutting tool. Reaching down a
+wall or into a pocket, the holder or shank can hit the part or a clamp
+before the tip does.
+
+## What CamCraft does
+
+A tool stores its diameter, flute length, shank diameter and length, holder
+diameter and length, flute count, edge material and whether it cuts to centre.
+A holder can also be a modelled body, a mesh or a drawn profile, and the
+checks then read the body instead of a plain cylinder.
+
+- **Reach is checked at generate time for drilling.** A drill may go no
+  deeper into material than its usable flute, and its holder must stay clear
+  of the stock along every move. Both refuse by name, before the path can
+  reach the post.
+- **Collisions are checked on the simulated program.** The simulation flags
+  moves where the shank or holder carries through material, where a move
+  runs the tool through a fixture, and where a rapid goes through stock. The
+  flagged moves are marked in the viewport, and a flagged program does not
+  post.
+- **Machine tool limits** (tool length and diameter the magazine accepts)
+  are checked against the mounted machine when it states them.
+
+What CamCraft does not have is a separate report of "the smallest inside
+radius in this part against your tool." A tool too large for a corner
+simply leaves material there; **Deviate** shows the material left, and
+rest machining with a smaller tool can take it.
+
+See [Operations](@/guide/operations.md) and the
+[glossary](https://neotech.github.io/Camcraft/guide/glossary/) for holder and stick-out terms.

@@ -0,0 +1,52 @@
++++
+title = "Toolpath strategy"
+description = "Adaptive and conventional roughing, climb and conventional milling, finishing strategies and rest machining."
+weight = 3
++++
+
+## The principles
+
+**Conventional roughing** clears a pocket in offset rings or a raster. At
+corners and when a ring closes, the tool suddenly engages more material, so
+the load spikes. Feed and depth must be set for the worst point.
+
+**Adaptive (constant engagement) roughing** shapes the path so the tool's
+engagement stays near a set limit everywhere, with arcs instead of sharp
+turns. Because the load is steady, it allows a deeper axial cut and a
+higher feed, and spreads wear along the whole flute length.
+
+**Climb versus conventional milling.** In climb milling the tool rotates
+with the feed at the contact point: the chip starts thick and ends thin. It
+usually gives a better finish and less rubbing, and pulls the tool into the
+cut, so it needs a machine without backlash. Conventional milling starts
+thin and ends thick, and pushes the tool away. Roughing a hard surface scale
+sometimes favours it. Climb is the usual default.
+
+**Choosing a finishing strategy by surface.** Steep walls suit passes that
+follow constant Z levels (waterline). Shallow and flat areas suit passes
+that follow the surface in a raster, because on a waterline pass the spacing
+grows as the surface flattens. Floors suit a single flat pass. Most 3D
+parts need both: split by slope, so each strategy cuts the surfaces it is good at.
+
+**Rest machining.** After a large tool, material stays in corners and
+narrow areas. A later operation with a smaller tool can be limited to
+just those areas instead of re-cutting everything.
+
+## What CamCraft does
+
+- **Adaptive** is an operation kind (2D), with a **Max engagement** angle,
+  **Forward step**, **Stock to leave** and a choice of how the tool returns
+  between passes. The 3D pocket also has an adaptive strategy per level.
+- **Climb milling** is a check box on the Feeds tab of the milling kinds.
+- **3D Finish** offers several patterns: Waterline, Parallel, Scallop, Radial,
+  Spiral, Contour, Project, **Steep/Shallow**, Flat, Pencil and Corner. Steep/Shallow splits the
+  surface by slope, with a setting for each side.
+- **Rest roughing** is a check box on the 3D pocket: a closing ladder cuts
+  what the levels leave standing. Across setups, the stock can be carried from
+  the previous setup so later checks see what the earlier one left.
+- Pencil finishing rides the concave corners that a larger reference ball
+  leaves standing.
+
+The full list of kinds and their settings is on the
+[Operations](@/guide/operations.md) page; ordering them is covered by
+[Order of operations](https://neotech.github.io/Camcraft/guide/order-of-operations/).
